clue.text: Girl wearing long mac unsettled poor poet

indicators.note: something unsettled has been disturbed out of its order, so these letters get rearranged
whoever is wearing clothes sits inside them, so one piece goes inside the other

blocks.note: the letters taken as written, ready to be rearranged
gal is an informal word for a girl

explanation.surface: A girl in a long raincoat is somehow unsettling a struggling poet.
explanation.walkthrough: William McGonagall, the Scottish rhymester of the Tay Bridge Disaster, is famous as the worst poet in the language; a mac is a British raincoat.
explanation.definitionFit: The Victorian versifier is proverbially the most dreadful writer of verse ever published, so a bad bard is exactly what he was.

clue.text: Eastern princesses I see rushed into short film

indicators.note: going into something means ending up inside it, so one piece is placed within another
cutting something short means losing its tail, so the last letter is dropped

blocks.note: a film of condensation or haze is a mist
the exclamation of sudden understanding
past tense of run, to hurry

explanation.surface: Princesses from the East have rushed onto the set of a short movie, as someone remarks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Short film' tempts you towards a movie; here film is a layer of haze, trimmed by a letter to become the outer shell.
explanation.definitionFit: Maharani is the Indian title for a great queen or a raja's wife, a royal lady of the subcontinent.

clue.text: African republic against holding up talk

indicators.note: in a down entry, whatever holds something up sits beneath it, fixing the order of the parts

blocks.note: gab is idle chatter
as in leaning on a wall, meaning against it

explanation.surface: A country opposes delaying the negotiations.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Holding up' reads as delaying, but in a down clue it means the lower piece supports the upper one.
explanation.definitionFit: This West African nation on the Atlantic coast, straddling the equator, is a sovereign state with a president.

clue.text: Never reprehensible solvers’ magazine now defunct

blocks.note: British idiom: behaviour that is 'not on' is unacceptable
the setter addresses the solvers directly, so theirs is 'your'
the famous American photo weekly that ceased publication

explanation.surface: A disgraceful puzzle magazine has gone out of business, and it will never come back.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain something that is 'not on' is out of order. Life was the celebrated American picture magazine, long since closed.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is an emphatic refusal, meaning under no circumstances whatever, which is how the single word works as a reply.

clue.text: Possibly become jolly having acquired rounds each

blocks.note: got means obtained or acquired
round letters, each shaped like a ring
the standard abbreviation used on price lists

explanation.surface: Buying a round of drinks for everybody might make you merry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jolly' pretends to mean cheerful; in naval slang a Jolly is a Royal Marine, a soldier who serves aboard ship.
explanation.definitionFit: Joining the Royal Marines means a life aboard ships, so taking to the ocean is one way of turning into a marine.

clue.text: Boy into minor sets of exercises

indicators.note: going into something means ending up inside it, so one piece is placed within another

blocks.note: lesser, smaller in importance
a son is a boy child

explanation.surface: A lad is getting into some junior workouts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Minor' reads as a youngster, which suits the boy, but here it means lesser in size or importance.
explanation.definitionFit: School lessons are periods of instruction, and textbook lessons are graded units of practice tasks for pupils.

clue.text: Either of two OT books briefly withdrawn before end of religious service

indicators.note: withdrawing means pulling back, so the letters retreat and run the other way
the end of a word is its final letter, so only that one is kept

blocks.clueFragment: Either of two OT books briefly
blocks.note: 1 Samuel and 2 Samuel are shortened to Sam in references
the final letter of the word

explanation.surface: One of a pair of Old Testament books is pulled just before a church service ends.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Religious service' looks like one phrase, but 'end of religious' gives a letter and 'service' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Mass is the Eucharistic rite of the Catholic Church, the principal act of worship held there.

clue.text: Cold-blooded type, foreign character divides churchless environment

indicators.note: without church means the usual abbreviation for the Church of England is removed
splitting something in two puts the divider in the middle of it

blocks.note: the surrounding atmosphere or setting; CE is dropped from it
a letter of the Greek alphabet

explanation.surface: An unfeeling foreigner stirs up division in a secular setting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cold-blooded type' suggests a callous person, but it means a creature that cannot regulate its body heat. CE, Church of England, is a common crossword abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: Frogs, toads and newts rely on outside warmth for body heat, making them ectothermic animals in the everyday sense.

clue.text: King enters rising river for sport

indicators.note: in a down entry, rising means reading upwards, so the letters run backwards
whatever enters something ends up inside it

blocks.note: the Tees is a river in north-east England
K is the chess and card abbreviation for king

explanation.surface: A monarch wades into a swelling river to amuse himself.
explanation.walkthrough: The Tees flows through Middlesbrough to the North Sea; read upwards it opens and closes around the king.
explanation.definitionFit: Skeet shooting is a clay-pigeon discipline where competitors fire at targets flung from two towers.

clue.text: Somewhat cracks tile in dwelling place

indicators.note: something that cracks a shell breaks in and ends up inside it

blocks.note: tile is old slang for a hat
a bit, meaning to some degree

explanation.surface: A roof tile on a house is showing some cracks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tile' reads as a roofing slab, but it is old slang for a hat, which gets broken into.
explanation.definitionFit: An animal's natural home or environment is where it lives, the surroundings it occupies.

clue.text: Tower made of alloy, last bit secured by drill

indicators.note: the last bit of a word is its final letter, so that one is picked out
something secured by a clamp is held within it

blocks.note: steel, an alloy of iron, without its final letter, which moves on
physical education, the school exercise drill
the final letter of steel

explanation.surface: A tower is built from metal, with the final piece fixed with a power drill.
explanation.walkthrough: Steel's last letter is detached and tucked inside PE, the school physical training once called drill.
explanation.definitionFit: A steeple is the tall pointed structure rising from a church, the spire together with its supporting base.

clue.text: Newton, under tree, catches Herbert going off seniors at Trinity?

indicators.note: food going off has spoiled, so these letters are mangled into a new order
in a down entry, being under something means coming after it
whatever catches something holds it, so another piece goes inside

blocks.note: the elder is a small tree bearing elderberries
the name taken as written, to be rearranged
N is the symbol for the newton, the unit of force

explanation.surface: Isaac Newton sits beneath an apple tree while a fellow named Herbert wanders off, all at Trinity College, Cambridge.
explanation.walkthrough: The Newton and tree picture points to Cambridge, but the Trinity meant is Trinity House, the body that runs lighthouses around England and Wales.
explanation.definitionFit: The governing members of Trinity House, the lighthouse authority, carry this historic title; the question mark flags the misleading college.

clue.text: Samurai warrior ultimately in on swapping places

indicators.note: ultimately means in the end, so only the closing letter is kept
things that swap places end up in a different order from the one printed

blocks.note: the final letter of the word
the two short words taken as written

explanation.surface: A Japanese warrior finally joins in, with two fighters trading positions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Samurai warrior' looks like a single definition, but 'warrior' only lends its last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A ronin was a masterless member of the feudal Japanese military class, one who had lost his lord.

clue.text: Result of heavy fall, maybe sort to involve present doctor

indicators.note: to involve is to take in or include, so one piece goes inside the other

blocks.note: to sift is to sort through
the present moment
the usual abbreviation for doctor

explanation.surface: After a bad tumble, a patient must sort out getting to see a doctor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Heavy fall' suggests an injury, but the fall here is of snow.
explanation.definitionFit: Heavy snowfall piles up in banks blown by the wind, so a drift is one possible consequence of it.

clue.text: Perhaps time spent working with arms race to maintain

definitions.text: Perhaps time spent working with arms

blocks.note: the Grand National, Britain's most famous steeplechase horse race
to service a car or machine is to maintain it

explanation.surface: Someone spends their time in a weapons industry that is racing to keep up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Arms race' looks like a set phrase, but it splits: 'arms' ends the definition and 'race' starts the wordplay. The Grand National is run each spring at Aintree.
explanation.definitionFit: Compulsory military conscription meant young men spending a period in uniform bearing weapons; 'Perhaps' marks it as one example.

clue.text: Rigid impression surfacing about new head of Royal Mail

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter, so just that one is kept
making something new means remaking it, so these letters come out in a fresh order
about means around, so one piece wraps the other
in a down entry, surfacing means coming up, so the letters read from bottom to top

blocks.note: a dent is a hollow pressed into a surface
the opening letter of the word
taken as written, to be rearranged with the letter before it

explanation.surface: A lasting mark is emerging over the appointment of a new boss at the postal service.
explanation.walkthrough: Royal Mail is Britain's postal service, but only its first letter plus 'Mail' are used. Build DEN-ILMAR-T, then read it upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Something constrained to run along fixed tracks, like a tram, is inflexible, so the word means stuck in an unchangeable course.

clue.text: Sneakily picked up things from kit that’s unopened and apparently locked?

indicators.note: something unopened has not had its front broken into, so the first letter goes

blocks.note: gear, meaning kit or equipment, without its first letter
wearing a wig, one has locks of hair, if only apparently

explanation.surface: Someone crept off with items from an unopened kit that seemed to be secured.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Locked' suggests a fastened box, but locks here are hair: someone in a wig only appears to have them. The question mark flags this.
explanation.definitionFit: To earwig is British slang for eavesdropping, so it means covertly overhearing conversations that were not meant for you.

clue.text: Friendly rowing mate, geek, mainly after spring loop that holds right bit

indicators.note: mainly means most but not all, so the final letter is lost
whatever holds something keeps it inside itself
one piece coming after the rest places it at the end

blocks.note: a spa is a mineral spring
a ring is a closed loop
the standard abbreviation for right
a part is a bit or portion
a nerd is a geek; its last letter is dropped

explanation.surface: A crew-mate in the boat, a bit of a nerd, is described as friendly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rowing' pretends to be about boats; it is rowing as in quarrelling, so the mate is one you trade blows with in practice. The right goes just after the ring's R.
explanation.definitionFit: A boxer trains against a sparring partner, someone who fights them for practice without real hostility.

clue.text: Wood, eg, one in North American story

indicators.note: being in something means sitting inside it

blocks.note: the abbreviation for North American
a tale is a story
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Timber, for example, features in an American folk tale.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wood' looks like timber, but the capital W, forced at the clue's start, hides a surname.
explanation.definitionFit: Natalie Wood was the Hollywood actress of West Side Story, so her first name is an example that fits the surname.

clue.text: French biologist beyond regret when back-tracking

blocks.note: past means beyond, as in past the church
to rue is to regret

explanation.surface: A French scientist is past regretting having retreated.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Back-tracking' sounds like a change of heart, but it only turns the second piece round.
explanation.definitionFit: Louis Pasteur, the nineteenth-century chemist and microbiologist, developed pasteurisation and vaccines for rabies.

clue.text: Moderates final section around enclosure’s borders

explanation.definitionFit: To palliate is to ease or soften something such as pain or blame, without curing it, which is what tempering does.
